1056:   // Events are handled in order per top-level session (a child's events with
1057:   // its parent's), but one session's slow hook never holds up another's
1058:   // events: a turn end stuck behind it would make the next prompt skip its
1059:   // turn-start. location.shutdown waits for every session's queue.
1060:   function enqueueEvent(event: any) {
1061:     const sessionID: string | undefined = event?.data?.sessionID
1062:     if (event?.type === "location.shutdown") {
1063:       const all = Promise.all([...eventQueues.values()])
1064:       eventQueues.set("", all.then(() => runEvent(event)))
1065:       return
1066:     }
1067:     const key = sessionID ? topLevelSession(sessionID) : ""
1068:     const next = (eventQueues.get(key) ?? Promise.resolve()).then(() => runEvent(event))
1069:     eventQueues.set(key, next)
1070:     next.then(() => {
1071:       if (eventQueues.get(key) === next) eventQueues.delete(key)
1072:     })
1073:   }

1075:   async function runEvent(event: any) {
1076:     try {
1077:       await handleEvent(event)
1078:     } catch {
1079:       // Silently ignore — plugin failures must not crash OpenCode
1080:     }
1081:   }

1083:   async function handleEvent(event: any) {
1084:     const type: string = event?.type ?? ""
1085:     const data = event?.data ?? {}
1086:     const sessionID: string | undefined = data.sessionID
1087:     switch (type) {
1088:       case "session.tool.progress": {
1089:         const childID = data.metadata?.sessionID
1090:         if (!tracked(sessionID) || !data.id || typeof childID !== "string" || data.metadata?.status !== "running") return
1091:         const key = callKey(sessionID, data.id)
1092:         trackChild(childID, sessionID)
1093:         if (taskStarts.has(key)) return
1094:         if (stoppedBeforeStart.delete(key)) return
1095:         const call = taskCalls.get(key)
1096:         if (!call) return // a call this instance never saw begin
1097:         const payload = taskPayload(sessionID, data.id, childID, call)
1098:         liveTasks.set(key, payload)
1099:         await announceTask(key, payload)
1100:         return
1101:       }
1102:       case "session.execution.started": {
1103:         if (!tracked(sessionID)) return
1104:         if (isChild(sessionID)) {
1105:           busySessions.add(sessionID)
1106:           endedUnheld.delete(sessionID)
1107:           return
1108:         }
1109:         // An execution with no prompt: OpenCode delivering a background
1110:         // subagent's result. The session takes a turn on it, with no prompt.
1111:         if (!activeTurns.has(sessionID)) await startTurn(sessionID, "")
1112:         return
1113:       }
1114:       case "session.execution.succeeded":
1115:       case "session.execution.failed":
1116:       case "session.execution.interrupted": {
1117:         if (!tracked(sessionID)) return
1118:         if (isChild(sessionID)) {
1119:           busySessions.delete(sessionID)
1120:           if (drainAtEnd.delete(sessionID) || type !== "session.execution.succeeded") drainBackgroundTasks(sessionID)
1121:           else finishBackgroundTask(sessionID)
1122:           return
1123:         }
1124:         if (type === "session.execution.interrupted") launcherInterrupted(sessionID)
1125:         endTurn(sessionID)
1126:         return
1127:       }
1128:       case "session.compaction.ended": {
1129:         if (sessions.has(sessionID ?? "")) runDetached(sessionID!, "compaction", { session_id: sessionID! })
1130:         return
1131:       }
1132:       case "session.deleted": {
1133:         if (!sessionID || !startedSessions.delete(sessionID)) return
1134:         endSession(sessionID)
1135:         return
1136:       }
1137:       case "location.shutdown": {
1138:         if (event?.location?.directory === directory) ending = endSessions()
1139:         return
1140:       }
1141:     }
1142:   }
1143: 
1144:   return async () => {
1145:     await within(Promise.all([ending, endSessions()]), v2CleanupWaitMs)
1146:     abort.abort()
1147:   }

This CLI is how you and your agents use Entire from the terminal — anything you do on entire.com, you can do here: - **Distributed Git hosting** — host repositories on Entire's Git-compatible server, or mirror your GitHub ones, and replicate them in regions around the world for data residency and the scale of agent traffic. → [Repositories & Git Hosting](#repositories--git-hosting) - **Trails** — instead of reviewing a diff, get a heads-up display for every change, with customizable evals that agents score on every push. → [Trails](#trails) - **Continuous memory** — capture every agent session as a checkpoint linked to your commits; [entire-brain](https://docs.entire.com/guides/brain/overview) combines them with [entire-graph](https://docs.entire.com/guides/graph/overview)'s code map into project memory. → [Agent Sessions](#agent-sessions) Works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot CLI, OpenCode, Antigravity, Factory AI Droid, Pi, and [more](https://docs.entire.com/agents/agent-integration-protocol/overview), and extends through [plugins](#plugins). Pushes through a GitHub mirror still trigger your GitHub Actions, and Trails can also show CI results from Buildkite and Depot. Open source under the MIT license. Docs: **[docs.entire.com](https://docs.entire.com)**. ## Contents - [Install](#install) - [Quick Start](#quick-start) - [Repositories & Git Hosting](#repositories--git-hosting) - [Trails](#trails) - [Agent Sessions](#agent-sessions) - [Search, Activity & the API](#search-activity--the-api) - [Plugins](#plugins) - [Security & Privacy](#security--privacy) - [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting) - [Documentation](#documentation) ## Install ```bash brew install --cask entireio/tap/entire # macOS and Linux curl -fsSL https://entire.com/install.sh | bash # macOS and Linux, without Homebrew irm https://entire.com/install.ps1 | iex # Windows PowerShell 5.1+ ``` For the nightly channel (prerelease builds with the latest changes): ```bash brew install --cask entireio/tap/entire@nightly curl -fsSL https://entire.com/install.sh | bash -s -- --channel nightly iex "& {$(irm https://entire.com/install.ps1)} -Channel nightly" ``` Requires Git on macOS, Linux, or Windows. Scoop, `go install`, and installing during a GitHub outage are covered in [Installation](https://docs.entire.com/installation). ## Quick Start **1. Capture agent sessions** — works in any Git repository, no account needed: ```bash cd your-project entire enable # pick your agents; installs their hooks and Entire's git hooks entire status # current sessions and where checkpoints are uploaded ``` **2. Put a repository on Entire** — sign in, then mirror a GitHub repository into one or more clusters, or create an Entire-native one. Mirroring needs the [Entire GitHub App](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/github-app-access) installed for that repository. ```bash entire login entire repo mirror add # wizard: pick repos and clusters entire repo clone /gh// --nearest entire project create # wizard: owner, name, region entire repo create --project entire repo clone /et// ``` Then `cd` into the clone and run `entire enable` there to capture sessions in it. **3. Open a Trail** — in a repository on Entire, on the branch you're working on: ```bash git switch -c add-rate-limiting entire trail create --title "Add rate limiting" entire trail show ``` ## Repositories & Git Hosting Entire hosts Git repositories on clusters in several regions, so agents can clone, fetch, and push against a copy near where they run. - **Region** — where an organization's or project's data stays: a jurisdiction such as `us` or `eu`, set with `--region` when you create it. - **Cluster** — an Entire Git host, such as `aws-eu-central-1.entire.io`. `entire cluster list` shows them; a repository can have copies on several. - **Project** — holds Entire-native repositories and belongs to an organization or a personal account. Repository and project commands take its plain name (`--project acme`); Trail commands take `et/`, and treat a GitHub owner as the project for its mirrors (`gh/`). - **Mirror** — a copy of a repository on one cluster. GitHub repositories are mirrored from their GitHub upstream, and native repositories can be mirrored to more clusters. `entire repo mirror` manages both. Repository references name their forge: `/et//` for an Entire-native repository, `/gh//` for a GitHub mirror, or a full `entire:///…` clone URL. ```bash entire repo create web --project acme # Entire-native, private by default entire repo mirror add /gh/acme/web --cluster aws-us-east-2.entire.io,aws-eu-central-1.entire.io entire repo clone /gh/acme/web --nearest # time each cluster and use the fastest entire repo remote add entire # add Entire to an existing checkout, beside origin ``` A GitHub mirror keeps GitHub as the source of truth: clones and fetches come from Entire, and pushes are forwarded to GitHub, where your GitHub permissions, branch protection, and required checks still apply. Clones use `entire://` URLs through the `git-remote-entire` helper that ships with the packaged installs; after that, it is plain Git. See [Repositories](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/overview) and [Mirrors in the CLI](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/mirrors-in-cli) for regions, mirroring, unmirrored branches, moving a mirror off GitHub, branch protection, and access. ## Trails A **Trail** follows a change from intent to merge. Instead of reviewing a diff, you get a heads-up display for it — the Trail's page on entire.com, or `entire trail show` and `entire trail watch` here — with findings from evals that agents score on every push. Each Trail has a number in its project, such as `#42`. ```bash entire trail create --title "Add rate limiting" --type feature # publishes the current branch entire trail list --project et/acme --status open entire trail show # the Trail for the current branch entire trail watch # stream reviews, findings, and runner events live entire trail finding # findings dashboard for this branch entire trail finding apply # apply a finding's suggested fix entire trail finding resolve -m "fixed in abc123" entire trail comment add -m "Should this cover the admin API too?" entire trail approve entire trail merge # merge this branch's change into its base entire trail resume 42 # continue Trail #42: restore its branch's sessions in your agent ``` Trail commands use the current repository's project (`gh/` or `et/`); pass `--project` or `--repo` to work on another one without a checkout. `entire trail list` always takes `--project`. Other subcommands are `checkout`, `link`, `unlink`, `update`, and `approvals`. **Project agents** are those evals: review agents such as risk, confidence, drift, security, and review, configured per project in Entire, which score each push to a Trail and raise its findings. `entire project agent` lists them and adds Entire's presets to your repository with `add`. Preset agents run on free credit; a custom agent runs once the project's billing is set up. ## Agent Sessions `entire enable` connects your agents and installs Entire's git hooks, keeping any hooks you already have. Use your agent and commit as usual: each commit that includes agent work gets a **checkpoint** — the prompts, transcript, and files touched — linked to the commit by an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer. Entire never adds commits to your branch; by default, checkpoints are stored as their own Git refs (`refs/entire/checkpoints/…`) and pushed alongside your code. ```bash entire checkpoint list # checkpoints on this branch entire checkpoint explain # the prompt, transcript, and files behind a checkpoint entire session resume # restore a branch's sessions and continue in your agent entire agent add # add an agent later; entire configure for other settings entire disable # turn capture off (--uninstall removes Entire from the repo) ``` See [Sessions](https://docs.entire.com/guides/sessions/overview) and [Checkpoint Storage](https://docs.entire.com/guides/checkpoints/checkpoint-storage) for how capture works and migrating from legacy branch storage, [Settings](https://docs.entire.com/guides/configuration/settings-layers) and [Git Hooks](https://docs.entire.com/guides/configuration/git-hooks) for configuration, and [Checkpoint Destination](https://docs.entire.com/guides/checkpoints/checkpoint-destination) for choosing the remote or a [separate checkpoint repository](https://docs.entire.com/guides/checkpoints/store-checkpoints-in-another-repo). Checkpoints are also the raw material for continuous memory: [entire-brain](https://docs.entire.com/guides/brain/overview), installed separately, combines them with [entire-graph](https://docs.entire.com/guides/graph/overview)'s code map into project memory your agents can query. From the CLI, `entire search` and `entire checkpoint explain` are the way in. ## Search, Activity & the API - **Search** — `entire search` runs hybrid (semantic + keyword) search over checkpoints, commits, and sessions, scoped to the current repo or `--all-repos`. `--json --compact` returns a trimmed shape suited to agents, and `entire checkpoint explain ` fetches the full detail of a hit. - **Activity and dispatches** — `entire activity` shows your activity overview, repository breakdown, and recent sessions from entire.com. `entire dispatch` writes a summary of recent agent work; `--local` generates it with your locally installed agent CLI instead of the Entire server. - **Raw API access** — `entire api ` makes an authenticated request to an Entire API and prints the JSON response, like `gh api`. It attaches your token and picks the host: `--to core` (the default) reaches the control plane (orgs, projects, repos, mirrors, clusters), `--to cell` reaches your home data cell (activity, repo aggregates), and `--jurisdiction ` reaches another jurisdiction's cell. `{owner}`, `{repo}`, and `{repo_id}` in the path are filled from the current repository's `origin`; `{repo_id}` needs a GitHub repository with an active Entire mirror. These endpoints are internal and can change without notice; where a purpose-built command exists, prefer it. ```bash entire api /api/v1/clusters entire api --to cell "/api/v1/me/recap?repo={repo_id}" entire api /api/v1/me ``` ## Plugins Any executable named `entire-` on `$PATH` runs as `entire `. Install plugins from the [plugin index](https://github.com/entireio/plugin-index) or any Git host: ```bash entire plugin search entire plugin install entire plugin list ``` Installs from a Git host are verified against the release's `checksums.txt`. See [`entire plugin`](https://docs.entire.com/cli-reference/plugin). ## Security & Privacy **Session transcripts are pushed to your Git remote** — as checkpoint refs, not commits on your branch. If that repository is public, anyone can read them. Entire redacts detected secrets before writing a checkpoint, but redaction is best effort; `entire checkpoint list --outgoing` shows what your next push will upload, and `entire checkpoint explain ` shows a checkpoint's contents. To keep transcripts out of a public repository, upload them to a separate private repository (`entire configure --local --checkpoint-remote github:/`) or stop uploading them (`entire configure --local --skip-push-sessions`). `entire enable` names the checkpoint destination every time it runs. See [Security](https://docs.entire.com/security) for redaction, scanners, deleting checkpoints, and cleaning up data from older versions. ## Troubleshooting | Issue | Solution | | --- | --- | | "Not a git repository" | Navigate to a Git repository first | | "Entire is disabled" | Run `entire enable` | | Agent hooks outdated after a CLI upgrade | Run `entire agent add `; add `--force` if that does not fix them | | A session stuck ACTIVE, or leftover session state | Run `entire doctor`, then `entire clean --force` if it persists | | Anything else | Run `entire doctor`; `entire doctor bundle` produces a redacted diagnostic bundle for a bug report | Set `ENTIRE_LOG_LEVEL=debug` for debug logs, and `ACCESSIBLE=1` for screen-reader-friendly prompts. Headless servers and CI: see [`entire login`](https://docs.entire.com/cli-reference/login). ## Documentation - **[docs.entire.com](https://docs.entire.com)** — guides for Entire and the CLI, including [how the CLI and entire.com fit together](https://docs.entire.com/platforms/cli-and-entire-com) - `entire help`, `entire --help`, and the [CLI reference](https://docs.entire.com/cli-reference); `entire agent-help` is the version written for coding agents - **Issues:** https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues · **Contributing:** [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) ## License MIT License — see [LICENSE](LICENSE).

# OpenCode

> Capture OpenCode transcripts, file changes, tool calls, and token usage with Entire

The OpenCode integration uses a project-level TypeScript plugin.

Follow [Set Up an Agent](https://docs.entire.com/agents/setup.md) for shared installation, verification, and troubleshooting steps.

## Add OpenCode

```bash theme={null}
entire agent add opencode
opencode
```

Entire writes `.opencode/plugins/entire.ts`. The plugin captures session and turn events, then uses `opencode export` to materialize the full conversation, file changes, tool calls, and token usage.

OpenCode supports commits before a turn ends. Entire refreshes the exported transcript so a checkpoint created mid-turn includes the agent activity available at that point.

## Limitations

OpenCode does not expose subagent lifecycle events. Entire captures the main session. `entire import` cannot import existing OpenCode sessions.

## Resume

`entire session resume BRANCH` restores the recorded session data when needed and prints:

```bash theme={null}
opencode -s SESSION_ID
```

See the [`session resume` command reference](https://docs.entire.com/cli-reference/session#session-resume) for flags and additional behavior.

=== attach help ===
Attach an existing agent session that wasn't captured by hooks.

This creates a checkpoint from the session's transcript and links it to the
last commit, or to the commit named by --commit. Use this when hooks failed
to fire or weren't installed when the session started, or to attach a
research session.

How the session is linked follows from two facts about the commit — does it
already have a checkpoint, and is it pushed — the same for HEAD and --commit:
  - It already has a checkpoint: the session is added to it. Git history is
    not changed.
  - It is already pushed: the commit is left unchanged and the link is
    recorded in a new checkpoint, which is pushed right away (under the manual
    checkpoint push policy it waits for 'entire checkpoint push'). The link counts
    once the commit's author attaches it, and names that exact commit: after
    a rebase or amend, attach the session to the new commit.
  - It isn't pushed: the Entire-Checkpoint trailer is added to it, which
    rewrites it and any commits after it on the current branch (their content
    is unchanged). A trailer survives a later rebase. Merges after the commit,
    or a rebase or merge in progress, are refused. If a remote can't be
    reached to confirm the commit isn't pushed, attach refuses rather than
    risk rewriting a shared commit.

attach prints what it is about to do and asks before doing it. Without a
terminal (an agent or a script) it changes nothing and exits non-zero; show
the user what it printed, and once they agree, rerun with --force.

A session can be attached to more than one commit. Each checkpoint records the
turns since the session's previous checkpoint.

Use --review to tag the attached session as an agent review. The
first user prompt in the transcript is recorded as the review prompt.
Pass --skills to declare which skills were actually run; omit to
attach a review without a declared skills list.

Works with any registered agent, including external agents enabled via
external_agents in .entire/settings.local.json (that file only, and only
when it is untracked). Run 'entire agent list' to see the full list.

If --agent doesn't locate a transcript, Entire auto-detects the agent from
the transcript and prints the detected agent name.

  entire session attach <session-id> [flags]

  -f, --force            Skip the confirmation. Only after the user has agreed to what attach describes
  -h, --help             help for attach
      --review           Tag the attached session as an agent review
      --skills strings   Optional: declare which review skills were run in this session. Only used with --review

The plugin loads fine in OpenCode 2.2.5 desktop (`opencode-cli serve --service`). Sessions are captured (2 OpenCode sessions in list), but our current quick-cactus session isn't recorded yet maybe because it started at 20:25 and no turn-end/end yet; Entire records session on session-start? The list showed only 2 OpenCode sessions, maybe from before. Hmm, our session is at 20:25; now ~20:39. It should have a session-start. Maybe OpenCode 2's plugin loader with `serve --service` doesn't support `location` per project? The plugin's entireSetup requires `ctx.location.directory`. If missing, setup returns early → no session-start. That might be exactly the issue: OpenCode 2.2.5's plugin API changed, so `ctx.location` no longer exists or `session.hook` API differs. Plugin silently fails → OpenCode sessions don't show up.

But then how were the 2 OpenCode sessions captured? Maybe by an older OpenCode version or by `entire` reading them via other means. Their started_at 19:06 and 18:43, ended 19:48 — around when? The plugin was committed 17:11. Possibly captured when they were started with the earlier plugin in v1 mode? But those session IDs are `ses_...` (v2).

So many OpenCode sessions attempted to register but only 2 have state. That points to plugin issues.

Meanwhile our quick-cactus session (started 20:25) has no lock at all — perhaps plugin setup failed for this worktree, or OpenCode 2 uses shared service and plugin setup for new location not rerun? Hmm.

The user likely sees "OpenCode .opencode/plugins/entire.ts (not found)" in Entire's web/session UI because OpenCode integration isn't recorded there. But locally, agent is enabled.

Critical finding: OpenCode 2.2.5 loads BOTH `.opencode/plugin/` and `.opencode/plugins/` directories! It tries to load the legacy plural file and fails because it lacks a default export (`Plugin must export a default definition with an id and an effect or setup function`). The legacy v1 file only exports `EntirePlugin` (named), no default. OpenCode 2 logs a failed-to-load warning. That's harmless but noisy, and could it break other plugins? It's a warning only.

But more importantly: restoring the legacy file causes OpenCode 2 to report "failed to load plugin" for it—exactly like the log showed for other worktrees earlier. Is that a problem? It's a warning, not fatal. But the user sees `.opencode/plugins/entire.ts (not found)`? Hmm, now it exists; OpenCode warns failed to load.

Wait, maybe OpenCode 2's own UI (plugin status) displays that line "OpenCode .opencode/plugins/entire.ts (not found)"? Hmm.

Hold on—the actual warning says "Plugin must export a default definition with an id and an effect or setup function. (cause: SchemaError(Missing key at ["default"]))". This is OpenCode 2 rejecting the legacy file. If The user's Entire UI lists plugins and shows this file as failed... not "not found".

Better solution: make the plural file a thin re-export with a default export that satisfies OpenCode 2, so it doesn't warn. But if it's a copy of the full v2 file, OpenCode 2 would load it too and run hooks twice! Unless it detects the singular copy and stands down. We could create a plural shim:

```ts
export { default } from "../plugin/entire.ts"
```
On OpenCode 2, both files load (as the log proves). The singular default is `{id, server, setup}`; the plural shim re-exports the same object → duplicate plugin id "entire" and double hooks! Bad. Unless the shim exports a no-op default for OpenCode 2 and the legacy plugin for OpenCode 1. E.g.:

```ts
import { EntirePlugin } from "../plugin/entire.ts"
export default process.env.OPENCODE === "1" ? EntirePlugin : { id: "entire-compat", setup: async () => {} }
```
But then on OpenCode 1, the singular file also loads and stands down (shadowedByLegacyCopy), plural runs the real plugin. On OpenCode 2, plural contributes a no-op plugin (no duplicate hooks), and singular runs the real server/setup. This resolves the load warning and keeps the path present for Entire's check.

But do we even need the plural file? For Entire's web check, any file at path works. Better to provide the shim rather than the 585-line legacy copy. The shim can import from the singular file and export the v1 plugin for OpenCode 1. However, importing the singular file on OpenCode 1 also executes its module-level shadow check? No, shadow check runs inside `EntirePlugin` when called. Import just defines. Then plural's default for OpenCode 1 is the singular's `EntirePlugin`, which when invoked sees `/.opencode/plugin/`? # Plugins

Write your own plugins to extend OpenCode.

Plugins allow you to extend OpenCode by hooking into various events and customizing behavior. You can create plugins to add new features, integrate with external services, or modify OpenCode’s default behavior.

For examples, check out the [plugins](/docs/ecosystem#plugins) created by the community.

---

## [Use a plugin](#use-a-plugin)

There are two ways to load plugins.

---

### [From local files](#from-local-files)

Place JavaScript or TypeScript files in the plugin directory.

- `.opencode/plugins/` \- Project-level plugins

- `~/.config/opencode/plugins/` \- Global plugins

Files in these directories are automatically loaded at startup.

---

### [From npm](#from-npm)

Specify npm packages in your config file.

opencode.json

```
{  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",  "plugin": ["opencode-helicone-session", "opencode-wakatime", "@my-org/custom-plugin"]}
```

Both regular and scoped npm packages are supported.

Browse available plugins in the [ecosystem](/docs/ecosystem#plugins).

---

### [How plugins are installed](#how-plugins-are-installed)

**npm plugins** are installed automatically using Bun at startup. Packages and their dependencies are cached in `~/.cache/opencode/node_modules/`.

**Local plugins** are loaded directly from the plugin directory. To use external packages, you must create a `package.json` within your config directory (see [Dependencies](#dependencies)), or publish the plugin to npm and [add it to your config](/docs/config#plugins).

---

### [Load order](#load-order)

Plugins are loaded from all sources and all hooks run in sequence. The load order is:

1. Global config (`~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`)

2. Project config (`opencode.json`)

3. Global plugin directory (`~/.config/opencode/plugins/`)

4. Project plugin directory (`.opencode/plugins/`)

Duplicate npm packages with the same name and version are loaded once. However, a local plugin and an npm plugin with similar names are both loaded separately.

---

## [Create a plugin](#create-a-plugin)

A plugin is a **JavaScript/TypeScript module** that exports one or more plugin functions. Each function receives a context object and returns a hooks object.

---

### [Dependencies](#dependencies)

Local plugins and custom tools can use external npm packages. Add a `package.json` to your config directory with the dependencies you need.

.opencode/package.json

```
{  "dependencies": {    "shescape": "^2.1.0"  }}
```

OpenCode runs `bun install` at startup to install these. Your plugins and tools can then import them.

.opencode/plugins/my-plugin.ts

```
import { escape } from "shescape"
export const MyPlugin = async (ctx) => {  return {    "tool.execute.before": async (input, output) => {      if (input.tool === "bash") {        output.args.command = escape(output.args.command)      }    },  }}
```

---

### [Basic structure](#basic-structure)

.opencode/plugins/example.js

```
export const MyPlugin = async ({ project, client, $, directory, worktree }) => {  console.log("Plugin initialized!")
  return {    // Hook implementations go here  }}
```

The plugin function receives:

- `project`: The current project information.

- `directory`: The current working directory.

- `worktree`: The git worktree path.

- `client`: An opencode SDK client for interacting with the AI.

- `$`: Bun’s [shell API](https://bun.com/docs/runtime/shell) for executing commands.

---

### [TypeScript support](#typescript-support)

For TypeScript plugins, you can import types from the plugin package:

my-plugin.ts

```
import type { Plugin } from "@opencode-ai/plugin"
export const MyPlugin: Plugin = async ({ project, client, $, directory, worktree }) => {  return {    // Type-safe hook implementations  }}
```

---

### [Events](#events)

Plugins can subscribe to events as seen below in the Examples section. Here is a list of the different events available.

#### [Command Events](#command-events)

- `command.executed`

#### [File Events](#file-events)

- `file.edited`

- `file.watcher.updated`

#### [Installation Events](#installation-events)

- `installation.updated`

#### [LSP Events](#lsp-events)

- `lsp.client.diagnostics`

- `lsp.updated`

#### [Message Events](#message-events)

- `message.part.removed`

- `message.part.updated`

- `message.removed`

- `message.updated`

#### [Permission Events](#permission-events)

- `permission.asked`

- `permission.replied`

#### [Server Events](#server-events)

- `server.connected`

#### [Session Events](#session-events)

- `session.created`

- `session.compacted`

- `session.deleted`

- `session.diff`

- `session.error`

- `session.idle`

- `session.status`

- `session.updated`

#### [Todo Events](#todo-events)

- `todo.updated`

#### [Shell Events](#shell-events)

- `shell.env`

#### [Tool Events](#tool-events)

- `tool.execute.after`

- `tool.execute.before`

#### [TUI Events](#tui-events)

- `tui.prompt.append`

- `tui.command.execute`

- `tui.toast.show`

---

## [Examples](#examples)

Here are some examples of plugins you can use to extend opencode.

---

### [Send notifications](#send-notifications)

Send notifications when certain events occur:

.opencode/plugins/notification.js

~~~
export const NotificationPlugin = async ({ project, client, $, directory, worktree }) => {  return {    event: async ({ event }) => {      // Send notification on session completion      if (event.type === "session.idle") {        await $`osascript -e 'display notification "Session completed!" with title "opencode"'`      }    },  }}
~~~

We are using `osascript` to run AppleScript on macOS. Here we are using it to send notifications.

If you’re using the OpenCode desktop app, it can send system notifications automatically when a response is ready or when a session errors.

---

### [.env protection](#env-protection)

Prevent opencode from reading `.env` files:

.opencode/plugins/env-protection.js

```
export const EnvProtection = async ({ project, client, $, directory, worktree }) => {  return {    "tool.execute.before": async (input, output) => {      if (input.tool === "read" && output.args.filePath.includes(".env")) {        throw new Error("Do not read .env files")      }    },  }}
```

---

### [Inject environment variables](#inject-environment-variables)

Inject environment variables into all shell execution (AI tools and user terminals):

.opencode/plugins/inject-env.js

```
export const InjectEnvPlugin = async () => {  return {    "shell.env": async (input, output) => {      output.env.MY_API_KEY = "REDACTED"      output.env.PROJECT_ROOT = input.cwd    },  }}
```

---

### [Custom tools](#custom-tools)

Plugins can also add custom tools to opencode:

.opencode/plugins/custom-tools.ts

~~~
import { type Plugin, tool } from "@opencode-ai/plugin"
export const CustomToolsPlugin: Plugin = async (ctx) => {  return {    tool: {      mytool: tool({        description: "This is a custom tool",        args: {          foo: tool.schema.string(),        },        async execute(args, context) {          const { directory, worktree } = context          return `Hello ${args.foo} from ${directory} (worktree: ${worktree})`        },      }),    },  }}
~~~

The `tool` helper creates a custom tool that opencode can call. It takes a Zod schema function and returns a tool definition with:

- `description`: What the tool does

- `args`: Zod schema for the tool’s arguments

- `execute`: Function that runs when the tool is called

Your custom tools will be available to opencode alongside built-in tools.

If a plugin tool uses the same name as a built-in tool, the plugin tool takes precedence.

---

### [Logging](#logging)

Use `client.app.log()` instead of `console.log` for structured logging:

.opencode/plugins/my-plugin.ts

```
export const MyPlugin = async ({ client }) => {  await client.app.log({    body: {      service: "my-plugin",      level: "info",      message: "Plugin initialized",      extra: { foo: "bar" },    },  })}
```

Levels: `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`. See [SDK documentation](https://opencode.ai/docs/sdk) for details.

---

### [Compaction hooks](#compaction-hooks)

Customize the context included when a session is compacted:

.opencode/plugins/compaction.ts

~~~
import type { Plugin } from "@opencode-ai/plugin"
export const CompactionPlugin: Plugin = async (ctx) => {  return {    "experimental.session.compacting": async (input, output) => {      // Inject additional context into the compaction prompt      output.context.push(`## Custom Context
Include any state that should persist across compaction:- Current task status- Important decisions made- Files being actively worked on`)    },  }}
~~~

The `experimental.session.compacting` hook fires before the LLM generates a continuation summary. Use it to inject domain-specific context that the default compaction prompt would miss.

You can also replace the compaction prompt entirely by setting `output.prompt`:

.opencode/plugins/custom-compaction.ts

~~~
import type { Plugin } from "@opencode-ai/plugin"
export const CustomCompactionPlugin: Plugin = async (ctx) => {  return {    "experimental.session.compacting": async (input, output) => {      // Replace the entire compaction prompt      output.prompt = `You are generating a continuation prompt for a multi-agent swarm session.
Summarize:1. The current task and its status2. Which files are being modified and by whom3. Any blockers or dependencies between agents4. The next steps to complete the work
Format as a structured prompt that a new agent can use to resume work.`    },  }}
~~~

When `output.prompt` is set, it completely replaces the default compaction prompt. The `output.context` array is ignored in this case.

# Plugins

Write your own plugins to extend OpenCode.

Plugins allow you to extend OpenCode by hooking into various events and customizing behavior. You can create plugins to add new features, integrate with external services, or modify OpenCode’s default behavior.

For examples, check out the [plugins](/docs/ecosystem#plugins) created by the community.

---

## [Use a plugin](#use-a-plugin)

There are two ways to load plugins.

---

### [From local files](#from-local-files)

Place JavaScript or TypeScript files in the plugin directory.

- `.opencode/plugins/` \- Project-level plugins

- `~/.config/opencode/plugins/` \- Global plugins

Files in these directories are automatically loaded at startup.

---

### [From npm](#from-npm)

Specify npm packages in your config file.

opencode.json

```
{  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",  "plugin": ["opencode-helicone-session", "opencode-wakatime", "@my-org/custom-plugin"]}
```

Both regular and scoped npm packages are supported.

Browse available plugins in the [ecosystem](/docs/ecosystem#plugins).

---

### [How plugins are installed](#how-plugins-are-installed)

**npm plugins** are installed automatically using Bun at startup. Packages and their dependencies are cached in `~/.cache/opencode/node_modules/`.

**Local plugins** are loaded directly from the plugin directory. To use external packages, you must create a `package.json` within your config directory (see [Dependencies](#dependencies)), or publish the plugin to npm and [add it to your config](/docs/config#plugins).

---

### [Load order](#load-order)

Plugins are loaded from all sources and all hooks run in sequence. The load order is:

1. Global config (`~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`)

2. Project config (`opencode.json`)

3. Global plugin directory (`~/.config/opencode/plugins/`)

4. Project plugin directory (`.opencode/plugins/`)

Duplicate npm packages with the same name and version are loaded once. However, a local plugin and an npm plugin with similar names are both loaded separately.

---

## [Create a plugin](#create-a-plugin)

A plugin is a **JavaScript/TypeScript module** that exports one or more plugin functions. Each function receives a context object and returns a hooks object.

---

### [Dependencies](#dependencies)

Local plugins and custom tools can use external npm packages. Add a `package.json` to your config directory with the dependencies you need.

.opencode/package.json

```
{  "dependencies": {    "shescape": "^2.1.0"  }}
```

OpenCode runs `bun install` at startup to install these. Your plugins and tools can then import them.

.opencode/plugins/my-plugin.ts

```
import { escape } from "shescape"
export const MyPlugin = async (ctx) => {  return {    "tool.execute.before": async (input, output) => {      if (input.tool === "bash") {        output.args.command = escape(output.args.command)      }    },  }}
```

---

### [Basic structure](#basic-structure)

.opencode/plugins/example.js

```
export const MyPlugin = async ({ project, client, $, directory, worktree }) => {  console.log("Plugin initialized!")
  return {    // Hook implementations go here  }}
```

The plugin function receives:

- `project`: The current project information.

- `directory`: The current working directory.

- `worktree`: The git worktree path.

- `client`: An opencode SDK client for interacting with the AI.

- `$`: Bun’s [shell API](https://bun.com/docs/runtime/shell) for executing commands.

---

### [TypeScript support](#typescript-support)

For TypeScript plugins, you can import types from the plugin package:

my-plugin.ts

```
import type { Plugin } from "@opencode-ai/plugin"
export const MyPlugin: Plugin = async ({ project, client, $, directory, worktree }) => {  return {    // Type-safe hook implementations  }}
```

---

### [Events](#events)

Plugins can subscribe to events as seen below in the Examples section. Here is a list of the different events available.

#### [Command Events](#command-events)

- `command.executed`

#### [File Events](#file-events)

- `file.edited`

- `file.watcher.updated`

#### [Installation Events](#installation-events)

- `installation.updated`

#### [LSP Events](#lsp-events)

- `lsp.client.diagnostics`

- `lsp.updated`

#### [Message Events](#message-events)

- `message.part.removed`

- `message.part.updated`

- `message.removed`

- `message.updated`

#### [Permission Events](#permission-events)

- `permission.asked`

- `permission.replied`

#### [Server Events](#server-events)

- `server.connected`

#### [Session Events](#session-events)

- `session.created`

- `session.compacted`

- `session.deleted`

- `session.diff`

- `session.error`

- `session.idle`

- `session.status`

- `session.updated`

#### [Todo Events](#todo-events)

- `todo.updated`

#### [Shell Events](#shell-events)

- `shell.env`

#### [Tool Events](#tool-events)

- `tool.execute.after`

- `tool.execute.before`

#### [TUI Events](#tui-events)

- `tui.prompt.append`

- `tui.command.execute`

- `tui.toast.show`

---

## [Examples](#examples)

Here are some examples of plugins you can use to extend opencode.

---

### [Send notifications](#send-notifications)

Send notifications when certain events occur:

.opencode/plugins/notification.js

~~~
export const NotificationPlugin = async ({ project, client, $, directory, worktree }) => {  return {    event: async ({ event }) => {      // Send notification on session completion      if (event.type === "session.idle") {        await $`osascript -e 'display notification "Session completed!" with title "opencode"'`      }    },  }}
~~~

We are using `osascript` to run AppleScript on macOS. Here we are using it to send notifications.

If you’re using the OpenCode desktop app, it can send system notifications automatically when a response is ready or when a session errors.

---

### [.env protection](#env-protection)

Prevent opencode from reading `.env` files:

.opencode/plugins/env-protection.js

```
export const EnvProtection = async ({ project, client, $, directory, worktree }) => {  return {    "tool.execute.before": async (input, output) => {      if (input.tool === "read" && output.args.filePath.includes(".env")) {        throw new Error("Do not read .env files")      }    },  }}
```

---

### [Inject environment variables](#inject-environment-variables)

Inject environment variables into all shell execution (AI tools and user terminals):

.opencode/plugins/inject-env.js

```
export const InjectEnvPlugin = async () => {  return {    "shell.env": async (input, output) => {      output.env.MY_API_KEY = "REDACTED"      output.env.PROJECT_ROOT = input.cwd    },  }}
```

---

### [Custom tools](#custom-tools)

Plugins can also add custom tools to opencode:

.opencode/plugins/custom-tools.ts

~~~
import { type Plugin, tool } from "@opencode-ai/plugin"
export const CustomToolsPlugin: Plugin = async (ctx) => {  return {    tool: {      mytool: tool({        description: "This is a custom tool",        args: {          foo: tool.schema.string(),        },        async execute(args, context) {          const { directory, worktree } = context          return `Hello ${args.foo} from ${directory} (worktree: ${worktree})`        },      }),    },  }}
~~~

The `tool` helper creates a custom tool that opencode can call. It takes a Zod schema function and returns a tool definition with:

- `description`: What the tool does

- `args`: Zod schema for the tool’s arguments

- `execute`: Function that runs when the tool is called

Your custom tools will be available to opencode alongside built-in tools.

If a plugin tool uses the same name as a built-in tool, the plugin tool takes precedence.

---

### [Logging](#logging)

Use `client.app.log()` instead of `console.log` for structured logging:

.opencode/plugins/my-plugin.ts

```
export const MyPlugin = async ({ client }) => {  await client.app.log({    body: {      service: "my-plugin",      level: "info",      message: "Plugin initialized",      extra: { foo: "bar" },    },  })}
```

Levels: `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`. See [SDK documentation](https://opencode.ai/docs/sdk) for details.

---

### [Compaction hooks](#compaction-hooks)

Customize the context included when a session is compacted:

.opencode/plugins/compaction.ts

~~~
import type { Plugin } from "@opencode-ai/plugin"
export const CompactionPlugin: Plugin = async (ctx) => {  return {    "experimental.session.compacting": async (input, output) => {      // Inject additional context into the compaction prompt      output.context.push(`## Custom Context
Include any state that should persist across compaction:- Current task status- Important decisions made- Files being actively worked on`)    },  }}
~~~

The `experimental.session.compacting` hook fires before the LLM generates a continuation summary. Use it to inject domain-specific context that the default compaction prompt would miss.

You can also replace the compaction prompt entirely by setting `output.prompt`:

.opencode/plugins/custom-compaction.ts

~~~
import type { Plugin } from "@opencode-ai/plugin"
export const CustomCompactionPlugin: Plugin = async (ctx) => {  return {    "experimental.session.compacting": async (input, output) => {      // Replace the entire compaction prompt      output.prompt = `You are generating a continuation prompt for a multi-agent swarm session.
Summarize:1. The current task and its status2. Which files are being modified and by whom3. Any blockers or dependencies between agents4. The next steps to complete the work
Format as a structured prompt that a new agent can use to resume work.`    },  }}
~~~

When `output.prompt` is set, it completely replaces the default compaction prompt. The `output.context` array is ignored in this case.

# Plugins

Add published packages, versioned packages, scoped packages, or local plugin directories to `opencode.json(c)`.

## Configure

```jsonc title="opencode.jsonc"
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "plugins": [
    "opencode-acme-plugin",
    "opencode-acme-plugin@1.2.0",
    "@acme/opencode-plugin",
    "./plugins/local",
    "../shared/plugin",
    "/absolute/path/plugin",
    "file:///home/me/plugins/local",
    {
      "package": "@acme/opencode-plugin",
      "options": {
        "agent": "reviewer",
        "strict": true,
      },
    },
  ],
}
```

Relative paths resolve from the config file containing the entry.

Configured local paths must be directories. A path to a single file is skipped. See [Load](/build/plugins#load) for
how OpenCode finds each part in a directory.

Plugin arrays from applicable config files are applied from lowest to highest precedence instead of replacing one
another.

```text
~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc
./opencode.jsonc
./.opencode/opencode.jsonc
```

## Discover

OpenCode also loads direct `.ts` and `.js` files and immediate plugin package directories from every discovered
`.opencode/plugins/` directory.

```text
.opencode/
└── plugins/
    ├── concise.ts
    ├── reviewer.js
    └── acme-package/
```

Global plugins use the same discovery layout under the OpenCode config directory.

```text
~/.config/opencode/plugins/
```

A `plugins/` directory beside a project-root `opencode.json(c)` is not discovered automatically; configure its plugin
directories explicitly or move it under `.opencode/`.

```jsonc title="opencode.jsonc"
{
  "plugins": ["./plugins/local"]
}
```

## Control

Plugin entries are processed in order. Prefix an ID or wildcard with `-` to disable it, use `*` for every plugin, and
use `.*` to match an ID prefix. A later ID re-enables a plugin.

```jsonc title="opencode.jsonc"
{
  "plugins": ["*", "-opencode.provider.*", "opencode.provider.openai", "-acme.reviewer"]
}
```

Two built-in plugins ignore removals so that a repository cannot switch off
[policy](/policies) enforcement: `opencode.config.policy` and
`opencode.provider.opencode`, the Console connection that delivers organization
policy.

## Manage

Install, list, check, update, or remove global package plugins with the CLI.

```sh
opencode plugin add opencode-acme-plugin@1.2.0
opencode plugin list
opencode plugin list --builtin
opencode plugin check
opencode plugin update
opencode plugin update opencode-acme-plugin
opencode plugin remove opencode-acme-plugin@1.2.0
```

`plugin check` checks server, GUI-only, and TUI-only package plugins for updates. `plugin update` updates every outdated package;
pass a configured package target to check or update only that package. Local plugins and exact package revisions are
skipped.

Package installation accepts npm names with versions, tags, or ranges, plus npm-compatible Git package specifications.
Git repositories can use hosted shortcuts, HTTPS, or SSH, including private repositories available through your existing
Git credentials.

```sh
opencode plugin add @acme/opencode-plugin@latest
opencode plugin add github:acme/opencode-plugin
opencode plugin add git+ssh://git@github.com/acme/opencode-plugin.git#main
opencode plugin add 'github:acme/plugins#main::path:packages/opencode-plugin'
```

Branches, tags, complete commit hashes, and npm's `::path:` repository-subdirectory selectors are supported. Configure
local paths directly; tarball and npm alias targets are not accepted by `plugin add`.

## Reload

Changes under watched config directories reload automatically. Server startup loads cached package plugins immediately,
installs missing packages in the background, and checks unpinned npm and Git plugins for updates without changing the
installed package. Exact npm versions and full Git commit hashes stay pinned. Changes to unwatched local dependencies
may still require restarting OpenCode.

```sh
touch .opencode/plugins/concise/index.ts
opencode service restart
```

## Desktop

A plugin that exports `./gui-experimental` also adds panels, commands, or settings to OpenCode Desktop. The app loads
plugins from the server it runs, so configure the plugin in your global `opencode.json(c)` to use it in every window.

```jsonc title="~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc"
{
  "plugins": ["opencode-acme-plugin"],
}
```

**Settings > Extensions > Plugins** lists them when the app's own server is selected. A plugin's switch turns off only
its desktop UI, and **Reload** loads it again after a failure. To turn off the whole plugin, add `-` and its ID to
`plugins`, for example `"-acme"`.

## Terminal

TUI-only plugins are configured separately and remain active when connected to a remote server.

```json title="cli.json"
{
  "plugins": ["opencode-acme-cli"]
}
```

<Card title="Build a plugin" href="/build/plugins">
  Create plugins that add tools, hooks, integrations, commands, agents, and other behavior.
</Card>

# Intro

OpenCode is an open source AI coding agent. It’s available as a terminal-based interface, desktop app, or web app.


## CLI

<CodeTabs
  id="install"
  label="Install method"
  tabs={[
    { label: "curl", code: "curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/v2/install | bash" },
    { label: "homebrew", code: "brew install anomalyco/tap/opencode-v2" },
    { label: "npm", code: "npm install -g @opencode/cli" },
    { label: "bun", code: "bun install -g --trust @opencode/cli" },
    { label: "pnpm", code: "pnpm add -g --allow-build=@opencode/cli @opencode/cli" },
    { label: "yarn", code: "yarn global add @opencode/cli" },
    { label: "vite+", code: "vp install -g @opencode/cli" },
    { label: "aur", code: "paru -S opencode-beta" },
    { label: "mise", code: "mise use -g opencode" },
  ]}
/>

The npm package uses a postinstall script to select the native `opencode` binary for your platform. The Bun and pnpm commands
explicitly allow the required script; Vite+ requires no additional flag. The mise command requires mise 2026.10.9 or later;
older versions install OpenCode 1.

Windows package managers are not supported.


Download a standalone CLI binary for your platform.

- **macOS:** [Apple silicon](https://opencode.ai/update/api/latest/cli/opencode/opencode-darwin-arm64.zip) · [Intel](https://opencode.ai/update/api/latest/cli/opencode/opencode-darwin-x64.zip) · [Intel (baseline)](https://opencode.ai/update/api/latest/cli/opencode/opencode-darwin-x64-baseline.zip)
- **Windows:** [ARM64](https://opencode.ai/update/api/latest/cli/opencode/opencode-windows-arm64.zip) · [x64](https://opencode.ai/update/api/latest/cli/opencode/opencode-windows-x64.zip) · [x64 (baseline)](https://opencode.ai/update/api/latest/cli/opencode/opencode-windows-x64-baseline.zip)
- **Linux (glibc):** [ARM64](https://opencode.ai/update/api/latest/cli/opencode/opencode-linux-arm64.tar.gz) · [x64](https://opencode.ai/update/api/latest/cli/opencode/opencode-linux-x64.tar.gz) · [x64 (baseline)](https://opencode.ai/update/api/latest/cli/opencode/opencode-linux-x64-baseline.tar.gz)
- **Linux (musl):** [ARM64](https://opencode.ai/update/api/latest/cli/opencode/opencode-linux-arm64-musl.tar.gz) · [x64](https://opencode.ai/update/api/latest/cli/opencode/opencode-linux-x64-musl.tar.gz) · [x64 (baseline)](https://opencode.ai/update/api/latest/cli/opencode/opencode-linux-x64-baseline-musl.tar.gz)

## Desktop

Download the latest OpenCode Desktop build for your platform.

- **macOS:** [Apple silicon](https://opencode.ai/update/api/latest/desktop/opencode/opencode-desktop-mac-arm64.dmg) · [Intel](https://opencode.ai/update/api/latest/desktop/opencode/opencode-desktop-mac-x64.dmg)
- **Windows:** [x64](https://opencode.ai/update/api/latest/desktop/opencode/opencode-desktop-win-x64.exe) · [ARM64](https://opencode.ai/update/api/latest/desktop/opencode/opencode-desktop-win-arm64.exe)
- **Linux (.deb):** [x64](https://opencode.ai/update/api/latest/desktop/opencode/opencode-desktop-linux-amd64.deb) · [ARM64](https://opencode.ai/update/api/latest/desktop/opencode/opencode-desktop-linux-arm64.deb)
- **Linux (.rpm):** [x64](https://opencode.ai/update/api/latest/desktop/opencode/opencode-desktop-linux-x86_64.rpm) · [ARM64](https://opencode.ai/update/api/latest/desktop/opencode/opencode-desktop-linux-aarch64.rpm)
- **Linux (AppImage):** [x64](https://opencode.ai/update/api/latest/desktop/opencode/opencode-desktop-linux-x86_64.AppImage) · [ARM64](https://opencode.ai/update/api/latest/desktop/opencode/opencode-desktop-linux-arm64.AppImage)


## Web

Access the OpenCode web interface with the `opencode pair` command.

```bash
$ opencode pair

  Open a link to connect. Links work once and expire in 5 minutes.

  http://127.0.0.1:49374/auth/connect/...
```

## Docker

Docker images use versioned tags, for example `ghcr.io/anomalyco/opencode:2.0.0`.

---

## Connect

OpenCode has built-in support for many LLM providers. You can connect to them
directly [in the TUI](/cli/providers) with `/connect`.

See [Providers](/providers) to configure custom providers.

If you'd like easy access to the best coding models, you can try out
[OpenCode Console](/console).

You can also try [OpenCode Go](/console/go), a $10/month subscription
plan that grants you access to the best coding models.

---

## Customize

Make OpenCode your own by editing the [OpenCode config](/config), [loading plugins](/plugins), [connecting MCP
servers](/mcp-servers), or [creating commands](/commands). For terminal interface themes and keybindings, see [CLI
settings](/cli/config).

---

## Learn

If you are interested in an in-depth course on OpenCode, Boot.dev has created an excellent [AI Coding with
OpenCode](https://www.boot.dev/courses/learn-ai-coding) course in consultation with our team. All the information in the course is
free to read and watch, though some interactive features may require payment.

```

Two built-in plugins ignore removals so that a repository cannot switch off
[policy](/policies) enforcement: `opencode.config.policy` and
`opencode.provider.opencode`, the Console connection that delivers organization
policy.

## Manage

Install, list, check, update, or remove global package plugins with the CLI.

```sh
opencode plugin add opencode-acme-plugin@1.2.0
opencode plugin list
opencode plugin list --builtin
opencode plugin check
opencode plugin update
opencode plugin update opencode-acme-plugin
opencode plugin remove opencode-acme-plugin@1.2.0
```

`plugin check` checks server, GUI-only, and TUI-only package plugins for updates. `plugin update` updates every outdated package;
pass a configured package target to check or update only that package. Local plugins and exact package revisions are
skipped.

Package installation accepts npm names with versions, tags, or ranges, plus npm-compatible Git package specifications.
Git repositories can use hosted shortcuts, HTTPS, or SSH, including private repositories available through your existing
Git credentials.

```sh
opencode plugin add @acme/opencode-plugin@latest
opencode plugin add github:acme/opencode-plugin
opencode plugin add git+ssh://git@github.com/acme/opencode-plugin.git#main
opencode plugin add 'github:acme/plugins#main::path:packages/opencode-plugin'
```

Branches, tags, complete commit hashes, and npm's `::path:` repository-subdirectory selectors are supported. Configure
local paths directly; tarball and npm alias targets are not accepted by `plugin add`.

## Reload

Changes under watched config directories reload automatically. Server startup loads cached package plugins immediately,
installs missing packages in the background, and checks unpinned npm and Git plugins for updates without changing the
installed package. Exact npm versions and full Git commit hashes stay pinned. Changes to unwatched local dependencies
may still require restarting OpenCode.

```sh
touch .opencode/plugins/concise/index.ts
opencode service restart
```

## Desktop

A plugin that exports `./gui-experimental` also adds panels, commands, or settings to OpenCode Desktop. The app loads
plugins from the server it runs, so configure the plugin in your global `opencode.json(c)` to use it in every window.

```jsonc title="~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc"
{
  "plugins": ["opencode-acme-plugin"],
}
```

**Settings > Extensions > Plugins** lists them when the app's own server is selected. A plugin's switch turns off only
its desktop UI, and **Reload** loads it again after a failure. To turn off the whole plugin, add `-` and its ID to
`plugins`, for example `"-acme"`.

## Terminal

TUI-only plugins are configured separately and remain active when connected to a remote server.

```json title="cli.json"
{
  "plugins": ["opencode-acme-cli"]
}
```

</Card>

OpenCode 2 docs: discovery is `.opencode/plugins/` (plural!) for V2, and `.opencode/plugin/` (singular) is OpenCode 1's dir. Wait, docs say "OpenCode also loads direct .ts and .js files ... from every discovered `.opencode/plugins/` directory." That's V2. Yet the log shows both dirs loaded. Hmm. And the Entire 0.12.3 installer writes `.opencode/plugin/entire.ts` (singular) claiming OpenCode 2 support. The plugin comment says OpenCode 2 requires the default export object. Contradiction with docs (V2 discovery plural). But the log shows V2 loading both.

Let's fetch /build/plugins (the plugin API docs) to see the export shape.

# Overview

Plugins modify OpenCode's behavior and add new features. A plugin is one package with a server part, a TUI part, a GUI
part, or any combination.

```ts title=".opencode/plugins/example/index.ts"
import { Plugin } from "@opencode/plugin"

export default Plugin.define({
  id: "example",
  async setup(ctx) {
    await ctx.storage.set("loaded", true)
  },
})
```

Migrating an existing OpenCode 1 plugin? Follow the [V1 plugin migration guide](/build/plugins/migrate-v1).

## Parts

Each part is an export of the package. Every part's SDK comes from the one `@opencode/plugin` dependency.

```json title="package.json"
{
  "name": "opencode-acme-plugin",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "type": "module",
  "exports": {
    ".": "./src/index.ts",
    "./tui": "./src/tui.tsx",
    "./gui-experimental": "./dist/gui-experimental.cjs",
    "./rpc": "./src/rpc.ts"
  },
  "files": ["src", "dist"],
  "dependencies": {
    "@opencode/plugin": "latest"
  }
}
```

- **Server** (`.` or `./server`) runs in the OpenCode server with `@opencode/plugin`. It adds tools, hooks,
  integrations, commands, and agents. See [Server](/build/plugins/server), or [Effect plugins](/build/plugins/effect)
  for the Effect API.
- **TUI** (`./tui`) runs in the terminal UI with `@opencode/plugin/tui`. See [TUI](/build/plugins/cli).
- **GUI** (`./gui-experimental`) runs its `setup` in every OpenCode Desktop window and its `main` in the desktop app's
  main process, with `@opencode/plugin/gui`. See [GUI](/build/plugins/gui).
- **RPC** (`./rpc`) is a typed contract that the server part implements and the other parts and clients call. See
  [RPC](/build/plugins/rpc).

The plugin's `id` comes from its server part's `Plugin.define`. A package with a GUI part and no server part takes its
package name (or a local directory's name) as its `id`. A TUI part declares its own `id`; a GUI part declares none and
takes the plugin's.

## Load

Plugins under `.opencode/plugins/` load automatically, like the local example above. To load published packages or
plugin directories from other locations, add them to `plugins` in `opencode.json(c)`:

```jsonc title="opencode.jsonc"
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "plugins": [
    "opencode-acme-plugin",
    "opencode-acme-plugin@1.2.0",
    "@acme/opencode-plugin",
    "./plugins/local",
    "../shared/plugin",
    "/absolute/path/plugin",
    "file:///home/me/plugins/local",
    {
      "package": "@acme/opencode-plugin",
      "options": {
        "agent": "reviewer",
        "strict": true,
      },
    },
  ],
}
```

- One entry loads every part. The TUI loads the TUI parts of the plugins its server loads, and OpenCode Desktop loads
  the GUI parts of the plugins in your global `opencode.json(c)`.
- A package with only a TUI part goes in [`cli.json`](/cli/plugins) instead.
- A local plugin directory with a `package.json` `name` and `exports` loads its parts through them, like the published
  package. Without them, it uses file names at its root: `server` (else `index`), `tui`, and `rpc` with a `.ts`,
  `.tsx`, or `.js` extension, and `gui-experimental.cjs` (or `.js`).
- See [Configure plugins](/plugins) for more loading and configuration options.

## Publish

A published plugin is an npm package with the `package.json` above. Its parts use the same default exports as a local
plugin.

```bash
npm publish
```

- Export `./rpc` when other plugins and clients should import your [RPC contract](/build/plugins/rpc) without loading
  your implementation.
- Build the GUI bundle before you publish, and include it through `files`. See
  [Build the bundle](/build/plugins/gui#build-the-bundle).
- Use versions compatible with the OpenCode release you target, and test the installed package, not only a
  workspace-linked copy. Publish a compatible plugin update when you adopt a newer API contract.

  </Card>
  <Card title="TUI" href="/build/plugins/cli">
    Add commands, routes, slots, and Markdown renderers to the terminal UI.

  </Card>

    Expose typed methods and events from the server part to the other parts and to clients.
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

But the default must be object. The conditional `process.env.OPENCODE === "1"` breaks V2 CLI because V2 also sets OPENCODE=1.

So we should fix the shape detection. How to know V2 vs V1 at module load? In V2, `OPENCODE_CLIENT` is set (desktop), and the docs say V2 plugin API import is `@opencode/plugin` not `@opencode-ai/plugin` (the file imports type from `@opencode-ai/plugin`, type-only so irrelevant). V1 sets OPENCODE=1. V2 sets OPENCODE=1 + OPENCODE_CLIENT? Let's verify V1 behavior from docs/source. Could check an OpenCode 1 install? The project has `@opencode/cli-linux-x64-baseline` 2.0.32 (V2). No V1.

Maybe V2 sets `OPENCODE_CLIENT` always (desktop/cli/tui). If V1 doesn't, use `process.env.OPENCODE_CLIENT ? object : function`. Let's verify by searching OpenCode v2 source on GitHub for `OPENCODE_CLIENT` and `OPENCODE=`. The repo is anomalyco/opencode. Use GitHub raw/search via fetch. Let's try fetching source files or use grep.app? We have websearch. Could clone shallow? Network. `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode /tmp/opencode/src` maybe huge. Use GitHub code search API needs auth. Use `https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/search?q=OPENCODE_CLIENT` HTML maybe. Or raw file guesses.

Alternatively, empirically: the V2 probe shows OPENCODE_CLIENT=desktop. The desktop service also sets it. V1 likely doesn't set OPENCODE_CLIENT (it's a V2 concept: client type). So condition:
```ts
const isV1 = process.env.OPENCODE === "1" && !process.env.OPENCODE_CLIENT
```
But what about V2 CLI via `~/.opencode/bin/opencode` v2.0.32? Probe used the desktop CLI with `--standalone`; OPENCODE_CLIENT=desktop. The user's v2 CLI may set OPENCODE_CLIENT=cli. Either way it's defined.

What about OpenCode 1.3+ which accepts the object via `server`? It sets OPENCODE=1 and probably no OPENCODE_CLIENT, so gets the v1 function (fine). Pre-1.3 also function. So the heuristic works.

```
Update the comment.

Also need `.opencode/plugins`? Not necessary for OpenCode 2; it loads singular. But docs say V2 loads `.opencode/plugins`. The log shows both. Keep singular.

Wait, why did the real desktop app service not set OPENCODE=1? Let's re-check /proc/7334 environ: it had OPENCODE_CLIENT=desktop, OPENCODE_DISABLE_EMBEDDED_WEB_UI, OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL..., but not OPENCODE. So conditional with `!OPENCODE_CLIENT` and `OPENCODE === "1"`: desktop → OPENCODE unset → false → object. CLI V2 → OPENCODE=1 & OPENCODE_CLIENT set → false → object. V1 → OPENCODE=1, no client → true → function. 

Now, does V2 CLI via `~/.opencode/bin/opencode` set OPENCODE=1 and OPENCODE_CLIENT? Likely yes. Test with probe using that binary too.

Also, the plural file: OpenCode 2 loads it and it exports object (since OPENCODE_CLIENT set) → no-op. OpenCode 1 loads it and exports function → runs. Good. Maybe the commit's trailer points to a checkpoint that was created by a **Codex** session and stored in the local repo's refs, but was later pruned? Let's check `git show-ref | grep entire/checkpoints`. We saw local refs in `.git/refs/entire/checkpoints` earlier. Let's list. Maybe RN exists under a different name or was deleted by a push/prune. The user's README mentions checkpoint `01M68W...` for the Experience gate? Actually README says Experience gate checkpoint `01M6874YH...` (VQ), which exists. The latest commit 2205774's trailer is `01M68W861F...` (RN) — created in the temp/first commit but maybe never pushed and then lost.

Could we recover the checkpoint object from the git object database by searching? `git cat-file --batch-all-objects --batch-check` and grep? Checkpoint refs point to commits with messages; the object may still exist unreferenced. Entire stores checkpoints as commits/trees. If the ref was deleted, the object may still be in the object DB until gc. We could search for a commit with a specific marker. But the checkpoint ID is in metadata, not object hash. Entire's checkpoint ref names map to IDs. If ref missing, the object is unknown. Could use `git fsck --lost-found` to find dangling commits and inspect. That's heavy.

Alternative: `entire checkpoint list` in each worktree might show the checkpoint (it reads the trailer and stores?). Let's check in witty-mountain: `entire checkpoint list`. If the checkpoint metadata exists locally in `.git/entire/...` but the ref is missing, maybe `entire doctor --force` can repair or condense. The two OpenCode sessions with 0 turns have no checkpoint anyway. The attach wants to attach to HEAD's checkpoint, which is the repo's latest commit checkpoint (RN) created by a Codex session. That checkpoint's ref is missing because the last commit 2205774 was made by Codex and its checkpoint wasn't pushed? Hmm, but commit 2205774 is on origin (pushed in 16ef0b1's history), and its trailer references RN. If RN was never pushed, the trailer is dangling on GitHub too. Entire handles this by refusing.

Could we use `--commit` to attach to a different commit whose checkpoint ref exists? E.g., attach to `HEAD~1` (9dd4b9e, checkpoint 01M68RS7WA... which exists remotely). That would link sessions to an older commit — wrong but maybe acceptable? Not for "all sessions".

Or attach to the new commit a77dd65 (our fix) which has no checkpoint and is pushed. If HEAD is pushed and has no checkpoint, attach creates a new checkpoint without rewriting and pushes it. That would work! For the current worktree (quick-cactus), we can fast-forward to a77dd65 (or attach with `--commit a77dd65`). For other worktrees, their HEADs are different commits, some with missing checkpoint refs. We could target the new pushed commit `a77dd65` for all sessions using `--commit a77dd65`? Attach checks out? `--commit` links the session to that commit. If the commit has no checkpoint and is pushed, it creates a new checkpoint (pushed right away) without rewriting. That would put all sessions on the new fix commit. Semantically, all these sessions are part of the project history and the fix commit is the latest; not perfect but avoids overwriting.

But `git fetch` the new main first so each worktree can see a77dd65. Then run `entire session attach <id> --agent opencode --commit a77dd65 --force`. This creates a checkpoint per session on a77dd65. The first attach creates checkpoint for a77dd65 and pushes; subsequent attaches "already has a checkpoint: the session is added to it" → adds sessions to the same checkpoint. That's clean! One new checkpoint containing all OpenCode sessions, linked to the fix commit.

Is that acceptable? It adds all sessions to one checkpoint on the fix commit. The user asked "add all sessions there". Yes.

But will attach find the transcript? It did (past the export). It will include files touched by each session; some sessions may have touched files not in a77dd65 (e.g., features from later commits that are already in 16ef0b1 → yes a77dd65 includes them). Most sessions were for features now in main. Some (gentle-otter, quick-cactus) may be in-progress/uncommitted. Attaching them could include file snapshots not in the commit but checkpoint stores transcripts/files independently, so okay.
